text.paragraph: Establishing primary care for long-term prescribed sleeping pills and stimulants that began in adolescence: a nonjudgmental assessment, a prescription drug monitoring program review, sleep, mood, anxiety and safety, nutrition, and contraception three months after childbirth. Concerns: She wants to stop needing pills to sleep and to work, without being made to feel she is to blame for them; She is afraid of being unable to sleep or perform during the change; She worries about her weight if she stops the stimulant. [S]

tr.td: Safe prescribing of controlled drugs: one prescriber and one pharmacy, a prescription drug monitoring program check before every controlled-substance prescription, a written shared treatment agreement, urine drug testing explained as part of care, seven-day supplies at first, a locked box, and take-back of unused capsules
Addiction medicine consultation to confirm the diagnoses, plan a safe barbiturate withdrawal and taper, and advise on stopping the stimulant

Supervised barbiturate withdrawal: a short hospital admission to change secobarbital to phenobarbital with withdrawal scoring and seizure precautions, then a slow outpatient phenobarbital taper of no more than about 20% every two weeks, slower toward the end, paused for withdrawal symptoms, illness or a major performance, never stopped abruptly; no benzodiazepine or Z-drug in its place; no alcohol
Stimulant: dextroamphetamine held at one fixed morning dose until phenobarbital is stable, then 5 mg for two weeks and stopped, with mood, sleep and appetite checks; no other stimulant

Insomnia: cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia as first-line treatment, adapted to late performances (a fixed wake time, a wind-down routine after shows, sleep restriction only after the taper is stable), with a sleep diary; no new hypnotic

Depression and anxiety: PHQ-9 and GAD-7 at each visit, sertraline, weekly psychotherapy, the Mood Disorder Questionnaire before the antidepressant, a structured safety assessment with a written safety plan, means safety and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, and safety review at every visit
Nutrition and weight without stigma: regular meals and snacks around rehearsals, a dietitian visit, no weight-loss target and no dieting drugs, and screening for disordered eating
Contraception that barbiturates do not weaken: medroxyprogesterone injection every 13 weeks, after a negative pregnancy test, with an intrauterine device as an alternative

Naloxone not prescribed: she takes no opioid, has no opioid prescription in the monitoring program, her urine test shows no opioids or fentanyl, and all her pills come from a pharmacy; naloxone does not reverse a barbiturate overdose. To be offered at once if an opioid is ever prescribed or any pill comes from outside a pharmacy
Work: taper steps scheduled away from major performances, a written plan for late nights and travel, and letters she controls
Change from secobarbital to phenobarbital under supervision without a withdrawal seizure or delirium
Four-day supervised admission; no seizure, delirium or severe withdrawal
Lower the phenobarbital dose slowly, at no more than about 20% every two weeks, toward stopping
97.2 mg a day at discharge to 32.4 mg a day at four months; two pauses when needed; taper continuing
Stop dextroamphetamine with a short taper and no return to it
Stopped after a two-week taper; tiredness for about two weeks, then better
Sleep six hours or more on most nights using CBT for insomnia
About six hours on most nights; rebound wakefulness after each dose step settles within a week
PHQ-9 14 to 5 at four months; response
Regular meals and weight she is comfortable with, without dieting drugs
Three meals on most days; weight up 3.5 kg to a BMI of 21.9; she says she feels stronger

list.item: Independent in all activities; groggy in the mornings and tired in the afternoons; works long days [S]
Alert, warm and quick, anxious at first and then candid; speech normal in rate; no signs of intoxication or withdrawal [S]
Mood low and worried; PHQ-9 14 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 13; Mood Disorder Questionnaire negative; no thoughts of suicide or self-harm now [S]

text.paragraph: Structured synthetic safety assessment on 1955-06-22: current ideation absent, intent absent, plan absent. Outpatient care with close follow-up. Risk factors reviewed without detail: past suicide attempts reported in earlier years, a sedative use disorder, depression, the months after childbirth, and the low mood that can follow stopping a stimulant. Barbiturates are dangerous in overdose, so means safety is part of the plan: she agreed to take the unused capsules from earlier prescriptions to a pharmacy take-back at the next visit, to keep the current supply in a locked box, and to receive no more than seven days at a time. No alcohol with the barbiturate. A written safety plan was made with her, and the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (call or text 988) was saved in her phone. Safety is reviewed at every visit [S]
